sections.name: Hook
sections.markdown:
One letter left. Just one — and it is not an exotic one hiding in rare words: it is the
sound of breath itself, the softest thing a throat can do while still saying something.
And the moment it lands, something you have been building since the second lesson of
this course is finished: the sound map you first met as a stranger's table — 13 vowels,
33 consonants, 2 dependent signs — has no empty squares. Today you learn ह; today the
alphabet completes.

sections.name: Previous Lesson Review
sections.markdown:
पिछले पाठों की पुनरावृत्ति — answer from memory *before* looking anything up.

1. व sits between which two English sounds — and what must the lower lip do, and not do?
2. श vs ष: each borrows its tongue position from a Chapter 3 row. Which rows?
3. **Write from memory** (self-dictation): भाषा. Which s-letter sits in the middle?
4. From v1.c02.l06: what exactly is the visarga's sound — and its two "never" rules?
5. The honest count from v1.c01.l02: 13 + 33 + 2. As of yesterday, how many of the 33
   consonants did you own — and which one was missing?

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answers</summary>

1. Between English v and w — व is /ʋ/: the lower lip approaches the upper teeth without
   pressing (no v-friction) and without w's rounding. Drill the middle.
2. श /ɕ/ takes the च-row's palatal position; ष /ʂ/ the ट-row's curled-back retroflex
   position. Never both "sha".
3. भाषा (bhāṣā) — the retroflex ष; both vowels long: भा-षा.
4. A voiceless /h/ — a light breath after the vowel; never voiced, never dropped.
5. 32 of 33. The missing one is ह — today's entire lesson.
</details>

sections.name: Historical Context
sections.markdown:
ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भः — the last letter, and the class it keeps.

The course's letter-collection began with अ — the voice, mouth open, nothing in the way
(v1.c01.l03). It ends today with ह — the breath, throat open, voice still humming. The
tradition's recitation order agrees: the varṇamālā closes on the four ऊष्माणः
(ūṣmāṇaḥ) — श ष स ह — and ह is the final letter of the whole garland
[REF:whitney1889 §§19–75]. Last lesson gave you the three hissing sibilants; today's
letter sits in their traditional class while being, phonetically, a different creature.
Both halves of that sentence are true, and this course says both:

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** The traditional ūṣman class is श ष स ह. Phonetically, श ष स are
> sibilants — noisy friction shaped by the tongue. ह is not a sibilant: its friction
> happens at the glottis, in the open throat, with the tongue doing nothing. The class
> grouping is the tradition's; the phonetic distinction is real; neither cancels the
> other. [REF:whitney1889 §§59–65]

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** The grammatical tradition's own name for the class explains
> the grouping: ऊष्मन् (ūṣman) means "heat, hot breath, steam" — these four are the
> breath-sounds, the ones you could warm your hands on. By breath, ह belongs completely.

sections.name: Scientific Explanation
sections.markdown:
वैज्ञानिक व्याख्या — the breath with the voice left on.

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** ह is /ɦ/ — a voiced glottal fricative: strong airflow through the
> open glottis while the vocal folds keep vibrating in a slack, murmured mode. It is the
> breathy voice you built five times in Chapter 3 — the ʱ of घ झ ढ ध भ — standing alone,
> with no stop in front of it. [REF:ladefoged2015], [REF:whitney1889 §65]

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** विसर्ग ः /h/ and ह /ɦ/ are one gesture with the voice switched off
> and on: both push breath through an open throat. ः is voiceless — the hand on the
> throat feels nothing; ह is voiced — the hand feels a buzz the whole way through.
> [REF:whitney1889 §65]

Three consequences. **You already own the hardest part:** breathy voice cost real work
in Chapter 3; ह is that skill with the stop removed — for once the new letter is
*easier* than its ancestors. **The visarga gets its partner:** the ः/ह pair becomes a
self-checking instrument under your hand (§9). **Between vowels, keep it murmured:** in
मही and बाहु the voice never stops — vowel, breath, vowel, one unbroken hum. English
anchors both twins: the h of "a**h**ead" is usually voiced [ɦ]; the h of "**h**ouse" is
voiceless — pick the right one [REF:ladefoged2015].

sections.name: Sanskrit Explanation
sections.markdown:
संस्कृतव्याख्या — the lesson's idea in the simplest possible Sanskrit.

हकारः ऊष्मा।
(hakāraḥ ūṣmā.) "*ha* is an ūṣman — a breath-sound." — ह ऊष्म वर्ण है।

गुरुः हसति।
(guruḥ hasati.) "The teacher laughs." — गुरु हँसते हैं।

इह रामः।
(iha rāmaḥ.) "Rāma is here." — राम यहाँ है।

One honest note: "Rāma is here" needs no word for *is* — the verbless nominal sentence
is complete, correct classical usage. The word अस्ति 🔊 exists, but its स्त is a
conjunct, Chapter 5's subject; until then, इह रामः says everything.

sections.name: Hindi Explanation
sections.markdown:
हिन्दी व्याख्या

आज का वर्ण आपकी ज़बान पर पहले से रहता है — हिन्दी का ह और संस्कृत का ह सगे भाई हैं। दोनों
में गला खुला रहता है, और आवाज़ की गूँज के साथ साँस बाहर निकलती है। तो आज मेहनत किस बात
की? नया सीखने की नहीं — तीन आदतें सँभालने की।

पहली, और सबसे बड़ी: बीच का ह निगल जाना। तेज़ बोलचाल की हिन्दी में दो स्वरों के बीच का ह
अक्सर घुल जाता है — "कहना" कैना-सा सुनाई देता है, "शहर" शैर-सा, "बहन" बैन-सी। रोज़ की
हिन्दी में यह बिलकुल स्वाभाविक है; पर संस्कृत में हर ह अपनी पूरी हाज़िरी माँगता है। मही
म-ही है — ह साफ़, गूँज के साथ; बाहु बा-हु; इह इ-ह। धीरे पढ़िए, गले पर हाथ रखिए, और हर ह
पर कम्पन महसूस कीजिए — कम्पन गया तो ह गया।

दूसरी: ह बनाम विसर्ग। दोनों साँस की ध्वनियाँ हैं, इसीलिए उलझन स्वाभाविक है। फ़र्क़ एक ही
है, पर बुनियादी: विसर्ग ( ः ) बिना आवाज़ की फूँक है — गला नहीं गूँजता; ह आवाज़ वाली साँस
है — गला गूँजता है। रामः के अन्त में हाथ को कोई कम्पन नहीं मिलेगा; हरि के आरम्भ में साफ़
मिलेगा। लिखावट में भी दर्जा अलग है: ह पूरा वर्ण है, पंक्ति में अपनी जगह खड़ा, अपने भीतर
अ लिए हुए; ः केवल चिह्न है — हमेशा किसी अक्षर के पीछे, अकेला कभी नहीं।

तीसरी, वही पुरानी साथी: अन्तिम अ। मोह "moh" नहीं — मो-ह; देह दे-ह; गृह गृ-ह। आख़िरी अ को
उसका पूरा हक़ दीजिए।

और अब वह बात, जिसके लिए यह पाठ हमेशा याद रहेगा: आज वर्णमाला पूरी हो रही है। पहले अध्याय के
दूसरे पाठ का नक्शा — 13 स्वर, 33 व्यञ्जन, 2 अयोगवाह — आज अपना आख़िरी ख़ाली खाना भर रहा
है। और एक मीठा उपहार साथ में: संस्कृत का गृह ही चलते-चलते, सदियों का सफ़र करके, हिन्दी का
घर बना है। आज जिस शब्द को आप पहली बार संस्कृत में पढ़ रहे हैं, उसी में आपका अपना घर भी
बसा हुआ है।

sections.name: English Explanation
sections.markdown:
One card today — and then the moment the whole volume has been walking toward.

### The card — ह, the voiced breath

- **ह (ha) /ɦ/ — voiced glottal fricative.** Open throat, strong breath, voice humming
  through it. English anchor: the h of "a**h**ead" — usually voiced between vowels — but
  *not* the h of "**h**ouse", which is voiceless (that one is your visarga). Hindi
  anchor: ह in हर and कहानी, spoken slowly — the same sound, minus the fast-speech habit
  of dropping it (§7, §12).

No tongue position, no lip work: ह is the one consonant whose mouth is entirely borrowed
— while the breath flows, your mouth is already shaped for the vowel that follows (§11).

### Worked readings

- **हिमालय** = हि + मा + ल + य → hi-mā-la-ya — /ɦimɑːlɐjɐ/ "the Himālaya". Four plain
  akṣaras, no conjuncts: the highest mountains on Earth, spelled with beginner letters —
  and the word is a picture: हिम "snow" + आलय "abode" (§13).
- **गृह** = गृ + ह → gṛ-ha — /gr̩ɦɐ/ "house". The ृ mātrā from v1.c02.l03 riding ग,
  then a full ह with a full final अ.
- **हसति** = ह + स + ति → ha-sa-ti — /ɦɐsɐt̪i/ "laughs" — verb four of the course,
  after चलति, भवति and वदति (कूजति stays with the cuckoo). A fifth, वहति "carries,
  flows", slips into today's list: वायुः वहति "the wind flows".

### The completion — no empty squares

In v1.c01.l02 this table was a preview you were told not to read. Read it now. All of it.

| समूहः · group | वर्णाः (IAST) | IPA |
|---|---|---|
| स्वराः · vowels 1–6 | अ आ इ ई उ ऊ (a ā i ī u ū) | /ɐ/ /ɑː/ /i/ /iː/ /u/ /uː/ |
| स्वराः · vowels 7–9 | ऋ ॠ ऌ (ṛ ṝ ḷ) | /r̩/ /r̩ː/ /l̩/ |
| स्वराः · vowels 10–13 | ए ऐ ओ औ (e ai o au) | /eː/ /ɐi̯/ /oː/ /ɐu̯/ |
| अयोगवाहौ · dependent signs | अं अः (aṃ aḥ) | homorganic nasal · /h/ |
| क-वर्ग · velar | क ख ग घ ङ (ka kha ga gha ṅa) | /k kʰ g gʱ ŋ/ |
| च-वर्ग · palatal | च छ ज झ ञ (ca cha ja jha ña) | /t͡ɕ t͡ɕʰ d͡ʑ d͡ʑʱ ɲ/ |
| ट-वर्ग · retroflex | ट ठ ड ढ ण (ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa) | /ʈ ʈʰ ɖ ɖʱ ɳ/ |
| त-वर्ग · dental | त थ द ध न (ta tha da dha na) | /t̪ t̪ʰ d̪ d̪ʱ n̪/ |
| प-वर्ग · labial | प फ ब भ म (pa pha ba bha ma) | /p pʰ b bʱ m/ |
| अन्तःस्थाः · semivowels | य र ल व (ya ra la va) | /j ɾ l ʋ/ |
| ऊष्माणः · sibilants + h | श ष स ह (śa ṣa sa ha) | /ɕ ʂ s ɦ/ |

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** The inventory is complete: 13 vowels + 33 consonants + 2 ayogavāha
> — exactly the counts promised in v1.c01.l02, now owned letter by letter. The two
> ayogavāha keep their honest label: categorically neither vowels nor consonants, they
> only ever lean on a vowel (v1.c02.l06). [REF:whitney1889 §§19–75]

Forty-six letters and two signs — read, written, produced against the tissue-and-throat
checks. The wall chart
(`planned:assets/images/volume-1/v1c04l03-varnamala-wall-chart.svg`) is this table made
poster-size: print it, and there is nothing on it you do not own.

And the oldest promise of all: नमस्ते (namaste), the course's first word, is न + म + स्
+ ते — and three of the four pieces are yours: न since Chapter 3, म since your first
writing lesson, ते since the dental row met the e-mātrā. The one missing move — writing
स without its vowel and joining it to ते — is Chapter 5's opening act.

sections.name: Pronunciation
sections.markdown:
उच्चारणम् — four drills, in order. Audio: 🔊
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c04l03-drill.mp3` (drills 1–2 + ह/ः pair test),
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c04l03-word-list.mp3` (drill 3 + dictation track),
`planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c04l03-full-varnamala.mp3` (drill 4 — the model
recital).

**Drill 1 — the throat switch.** Hand on the throat. अः: a clean voiceless puff —
nothing under the hand. Now हा: the same breath with the voice on — the hand buzzes
start to finish. Alternate slowly: अः — हा — अः — हा, feeling the switch flip. Then the
word pair: नमः (ends voiceless) — हरि (begins voiced).

**Drill 2 — the murmur bridge.** The Chapter 3 transfer: say घ, feel the breathy
release; now delete the ग-closure and keep only the release — that lingering murmured
breath *is* ह. Then between vowels, without breaking the hum: इह — मही — बाहु. The voice
never stops mid-word: vowel, breath, vowel, one thread of sound.

**Drill 3 — syllables, then words.** Read across, one beat per short vowel, two per
long: ह हा हि ही हु हू हे हो. Then the §14 list from the audio, each word twice. Finish
with the danger sets: मोह, देह, गृह (final vowels full) and मही, बाहु, इह (medial ह held
voiced).

**Drill 4 — THE FULL RECITAL.** The lesson's centerpiece. With the model audio, recite
the complete varṇamālā in traditional order, group by group, a breath between groups:

अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ॠ ऌ ए ऐ ओ औ — अं अः — क ख ग घ ङ — च छ ज झ ञ — ट ठ ड ढ ण — त थ द ध न —
प फ ब भ म — य र ल व — श ष स ह

Three rounds: reading from the §8 table; from the wall chart across the room; then eyes
closed. Accuracy first — every aspirate breathed, every retroflex curled. Speed is not
today's goal; the timed version is lesson 4's exam.

sections.name: IPA
sections.markdown:
The formal value: ह /ɦ/ — voiced glottal fricative. Its voiceless partner: विसर्ग /h/.

**One phonation, two spellings:** the superscript ʱ (घ /gʱ/, भ /bʱ/) and the standalone
ɦ are the same murmured voice — ʱ rides a stop's release, ɦ stands alone. You have been
producing [ɦ] inside every breathy stop since Chapter 3.

**Narrow notes:** between vowels ह keeps full voicing — मही [mɐɦiː], बाहु [bɑːɦu] — the
murmur at its softest, and the sound easiest to lose (§12). In careful pause-form
reading गुरुः हसति is [guɾuh ɦɐsɐt̪i]: a voiceless breath closing the first word, a
voiced one opening the second — the whole ः/ɦ contrast in four syllables.

**Word transcriptions:** हिमालय /ɦimɑːlɐjɐ/ · गृह /gr̩ɦɐ/ (syllabic r̩ from ऋ's mātrā)
· हसति /ɦɐsɐt̪i/ · इह /iɦɐ/.

sections.name: Mouth Position
sections.markdown:
मुखस्थानम् — the letter card
(`planned:assets/images/volume-1/v1c04l03-ha-card.svg`) shows today's articulation — or
rather, the absence of one.

1. **Nothing to place.** Tongue at rest, lips relaxed: ह has no contact point in the
   mouth. The action is in the throat: glottis open enough for strong airflow, vocal
   folds slack enough to keep humming through it.
2. **The borrowed mouth.** Mirror up: say हा, ही, हू slowly. Watch the mouth take the
   *vowel's* shape already during the breath — wide for हा, spread for ही, rounded for
   हू. ह is a breath poured into the next vowel's mould.
3. **The instrument panel.** Throat-hand: buzzing throughout (silence means you made the
   visarga instead). Palm: steady warm airflow, no burst — there is no closure to
   release. Tissue: a gentle lean, never a jump.

sections.name: Common Mistakes
sections.markdown:
सामान्य-भ्रान्तयः — real errors, each with its fix. These feed the quiz distractors.

1. **ह devoiced to English house-h everywhere (mostly English speakers).** Every ह comes
   out voiceless, and the murmur is lost. *Fix:* the throat switch (§9 drill 1) — the
   hand must buzz through every ह; if रामः and हरि feel the same under your hand, the
   switch is stuck.
2. **ह dropped between vowels (mostly Hindi speakers).** The कहना-habit: मही slides
   toward [mɐiː], बाहु toward [bɑːu]. Natural Hindi — but in Sanskrit the ह is
   meaning-bearing and stays. *Fix:* the murmur bridge (§9 drill 2), slow: म-ही, बा-हु,
   इ-ह — one unbroken hum with the breath audible inside it.
3. **The letter ह confused with the sign ः.** Both get called "the breath", and notes
   start showing रामह-style errors. *Fix:* two absolutes — sound: ह voiced, ः voiceless;
   writing: ह stands in the row and carries अ, ः only ever follows an akṣara.
4. **The recital raced.** Completion-day excitement turns the varṇamālā into a speed
   run, and the aspirates flatten first. *Fix:* accuracy has right of way — group by
   group, a breath between groups. The clock appears in lesson 4's exam, and even there
   errors cost more than seconds.

sections.name: Examples
sections.markdown:
उदाहरणानि — three stories hiding in the word list.

### हिमालय — the word the world knows

**हिमालय** (himālaya) "the Himālaya" — हिमालय · /ɦimɑːlɐjɐ/

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** हिमालय is a transparent compound: हिम (hima) "snow" + आलय (ālaya)
> "abode, dwelling" — "the abode of snow". And English *Himalaya* is a genuine
> **loanword**: English borrowed the mountain range's Sanskrit name whole — like *yoga*
> and *karma*, a loan, not a cognate. [REF:apte1890 s.v. हिमालय]

Remember lesson 1's rule: a loan is handed over; cognates are siblings from one
ancestor. मातृ and *mother* are cognates; हिमालय and *Himalaya* are the same word, lent.
Today the borrowed name becomes readable in its own script.

### गृह and घर — one word's long walk

**गृह** (gṛha) "house" — घर · /gr̩ɦɐ/

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** Sanskrit गृह is the ancestor of Hindi घर: the modern word descends
> from the ancient one through the regular sound changes of Indo-Aryan. [REF:masica1991]

One line, but savor it: your everyday word for *home* is today's Sanskrit word, worn
smooth by some twenty centuries of mouths.

### मही and भूमि — collecting earth-words

**मही** (mahī) "the earth" — धरती · /mɐɦiː/

Chapter 3 gave you भूमि (bhūmi) "earth, ground"; today मही joins it — near-synonyms, and
your first taste of a Sanskrit habit: rich stocks of synonyms that poetry draws on
freely [REF:apte1890 s.v. मही]. Start a collection page: earth-words, two entries. (And
no etymology story for बाहु "arm" — this course only tells the ones it has verified.)

sections.name: Vocabulary
sections.markdown:
शब्दावली — fourteen words, every one readable; your readable stock passes one hundred
and thirty-five. Audio: 🔊 `planned:assets/audio/volume-1/v1c04l03-word-list.mp3` (model
reading, each word twice, plus the dictation track). Stems are listed bare, as always;
sentences dress subjects with ः (§8).

| देवनागरी | IAST | IPA | English | हिन्दी | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| हरि | hari | /ɦɐɾi/ | Hari; tawny | हरि | name-word — register note in §15 |
| हर | hara | /ɦɐɾɐ/ | Hara; taking away | हर | name-word pair of हरि (§15) |
| हल | hala | /ɦɐlɐ/ | plough | हल | the farmer's tool |
| हित | hita | /ɦit̪ɐ/ | beneficial, good | हित, भलाई | final अ full: *hita* |
| हिम | hima | /ɦimɐ/ | snow, cold | हिम, बर्फ़ | first half of the mountain (§13) |
| हिमालय | himālaya | /ɦimɑːlɐjɐ/ | the Himālaya | हिमालय | हिम + आलय "snow-abode" (§13) |
| मही | mahī | /mɐɦiː/ | the earth | धरती | beside भूमि (§13); medial ह stays (§12) |
| बाहु | bāhu | /bɑːɦu/ | arm | बाँह, भुजा | medial ह stays voiced |
| मोह | moha | /moːɦɐ/ | delusion | मोह | *moha*, never "moh" |
| देह | deha | /d̪eːɦɐ/ | body | देह, शरीर | pure long ए, full final अ |
| गृह | gṛha | /gr̩ɦɐ/ | house | घर | ancestor of Hindi घर (§13); गृ = ग + ृ |
| इह | iha | /iɦɐ/ | here | यहाँ | sentence-word (§6): इह रामः |
| हसति | hasati | /ɦɐsɐt̪i/ | laughs | हँसता है | verb 4 (§8); गुरुः हसति |
| वहति | vahati | /ʋɐɦɐt̪i/ | carries, flows | बहता है; ले जाता है | verb 5; वायुः वहति |

Reading protocol, as always: block by block (हि-मा-ल-य), then the whole word, then the
audio. Throat-hand on every ह; no ह dropped, no final vowel clipped.

sections.name: Grammar
sections.markdown:
व्याकरणम् — in Volume 1 this is a **script rule**: one new letter, and the script's
closing law.

### Stroke order — ह

Course convention as ever — body first, headline last; the stroke card
(`planned:assets/images/volume-1/v1c04l03-stroke-order.svg`) is the authority, and
traditions vary in details.

- **ह** — one continuous body: start just below headline height with a small leftward
  hook, sweep down and around into the open bowl, and finish in the curl at the lower
  left with its short inner tick; headline last. Like द, ह is a round letter — **no
  right-hand vertical stem** — so mātrās attach to the body: हि wraps in front, ही hooks
  behind and over, हा stands its post to the right, हु tucks its hook close under the
  tail. Fonts vary in the details; the stroke card is the model.
- **ह vs ः — letter vs sign, on paper.** ह stands in the writing line as a full akṣara
  and carries the inherent अ; ः is two small dots that only ever follow a finished
  akṣara. An "h" opening a word must be ह; the breath trailing रामः must be ः.

### The closing law — the inventory is complete

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** With ह, the letter inventory is closed: 46 letters and 2 signs.
> Everything else you will ever read on a Sanskrit page is built from these by
> combination — the mātrā forms you already command, and the consonant joinings
> (conjuncts) that Chapter 5 opens. New combinations are coming; new letters are not.
> [REF:whitney1889 §§19–75]

(Plus a couple of editorial marks in due course: ॐ you own already; the avagraha ऽ
arrives with sandhi in Volume 3.)

### हरि and हर — the name-words, honestly labeled

> **[FACT · तथ्यम्]** As dictionary words: हरि means "tawny, bay-colored" among other
> senses, and is a proper name; हर means "taking away, removing, seizing", and is a
> proper name. [REF:apte1890 s.v. हरि]

> **[TRADITION · परम्परा]** In the devotional tradition हरि is a beloved name of Viṣṇu
> and हर of Śiva — paired to this day in the compound हरिहर (harihara). In this lesson
> both are vocabulary, doing honest secular work.

sections.name: Conversation
sections.markdown:
सम्भाषणम् — someone is laughing in the next room. 🔊 audio recorded into the Chapter 4
drill pack (§27).

— कः हसति?
(kaḥ hasati?) "Who is laughing?" — कौन हँस रहा है?

— गुरुः हसति!
(guruḥ hasati!) "The teacher is laughing!" — गुरु हँस रहे हैं!

— इह?
(iha?) "Here?" — यहाँ?

— आम्! इह!
(ām! iha!) "Yes — here!" — हाँ! यहाँ!

Housekeeping, honestly: कः has been readable since v1.c02.l06 — the question word that
made the visarga famous — and every other word above is self-read. Only आम् 🔊 stays an
ear-word: its final म् needs the virāma, Chapter 5's very first gift.

sections.name: Story
sections.markdown:
कथा — हिमालयः · At the Snow-Abode. The course's cast takes a trip; six lines; each
line: Devanagari, IAST, English, Hindi.

1. इह हिमालयः।
   (iha himālayaḥ.) "Here is the Himālaya." — यह रहा हिमालय।
2. वायुः वहति।
   (vāyuḥ vahati.) "The wind flows." — हवा बहती है।
3. बालकः — हिम! हिम!
   (bālakaḥ — hima! hima!) "The boy: 'Snow! Snow!'" — बालक — बर्फ़! बर्फ़!
4. गुरुः हसति।
   (guruḥ hasati.) "The teacher laughs." — गुरु हँसते हैं।
5. ततः कोकिलः कूजति।
   (tataḥ kokilaḥ kūjati.) "Then a cuckoo coos." — तभी कोयल कूकती है।
6. बालकः हसति। गुरुः हसति।
   (bālakaḥ hasati. guruḥ hasati.) "The boy laughs. The teacher laughs." — बालक हँसता
   है। गुरु हँसते हैं।

The shout हिम! is the naming form, like फल! in Chapter 3 — a full sentence would need
हिमम्, whose final म् waits for Chapter 5. And now the meta-moment, worth a pause: every
letter in this story's Sanskrit is yours. Not most — every one. From today, nothing in
this volume's Sanskrit will ever again contain a letter you have not learned. New
*joinings*, yes — Chapter 5 is full of them. New letters — never again.

sections.name: Exercises
sections.markdown:
अभ्यासाः — six exercises; 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 are production tasks. Do them in order.

**अभ्यासः 1 · वर्णमाला-लेखनम् (the big one — write the alphabet, production).** Blank
sheet. Write the complete varṇamālā from memory, in traditional order: 13 vowels, अं अः,
the five vargas row by row, य र ल व, श ष स ह. Time yourself, but today the clock only
observes: accuracy is the bar. Check against §8's table cell by cell; mark every slip.
Lesson 4's exam repeats this with a bar of 8 minutes — today's errors are tomorrow's
checklist.

**अभ्यासः 2 · पूर्ण-पाठः (the recital, record — production).** Record yourself reciting
the full varṇamālā (§9 drill 4), then play it against the model audio 🔊 group by group.
Mark hesitations and swaps. Checklist: aspirates breathed? Retroflexes curled? य र ल व
in order? श ष स ह distinct — and ह voiced?

**अभ्यासः 3 · श्रुतलेखनम् (dictation, production).** Play the dictation track 🔊 (in the
word-list audio): ten §14 words in random order, each read twice with a writing pause.
Write them in Devanagari. Self-check against §14: every medial ह written? गृ with its ृ?
Long mātrās long? 8/10 is a pass; re-take tomorrow either way (§20).

**अभ्यासः 4 · अनुलेखनम् (tracing & writing, production).** Print the tracing worksheet ✍
(`planned:assets/worksheets/volume-1/v1c04l03-tracing.pdf`): trace ह five times
following the stroke arrows, then हरि, गृह, मही, बाहु, हिमालय unaided, then the sentence
row — रामः वदति। गुरुः हसति। वायुः वहति। — daṇḍa included.

**अभ्यासः 5 · श्रवणभेदः (ह/ः discrimination, written answers).** Play the pair-test
track 🔊 (in the drill audio): twelve breaths, each voiced (ह-type) or voiceless
(ः-type), random order. Write ह or ः for each. 10/12 is a pass; below that, rerun the
throat switch (§9 drill 1) and retest tomorrow — the ear sharpens overnight.

**अभ्यासः 6 · वाक्य-वाचनम् (sentence reading, record — production).** Word tiles: रामः,
गुरुः, बालकः, कविः, वायुः · वदति, हसति, चलति, वहति. (a) Read the sentence set aloud in
pause form and record it: रामः वदति। गुरुः हसति। वायुः वहति। (b) Assemble **two new
sentences** — keep predicates honest: वहति belongs to the wind, the rest walk with
anyone — write them with daṇḍas, and record those too. Compare with the model sentences
🔊: every word complete, visarga breathed, every ह voiced.

sections.name: Quiz
sections.markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. The sound of ह is: (a) a voiceless breath, like English *house*-h, in all positions
   (b) /ɦ/ — a breath with the voice buzzing through it (c) a sibilant like स (d) a
   vowel
2. According to the traditional classification, ह belongs to: (a) the antaḥstha, with
   य र ल व (b) the ūṣman class श ष स ह — though phonetically it is not a sibilant
   (c) the प-वर्ग (d) the vowels
3. Hand on your throat through रामः and then हरि. You should feel: (a) a buzz during
   both breaths (b) silence during the ः breath, a buzz during ह (c) a buzz during ः
   only (d) nothing in either
4. The completed varṇamālā counts: (a) 14 vowels + 32 consonants (b) 13 vowels + 33
   consonants + 2 ayogavāha (c) 13 vowels + 33 consonants, nothing else (d) 50 letters,
   all one category
5. A learner reads मही as [mɐiː] and बाहु as [bɑːu]. What happened? (a) nothing — both
   are correct (b) the ह between vowels was dropped — a Hindi fast-speech habit (c) the
   vowel lengths were wrong (d) the words contain conjuncts
6. In writing, the difference between ह and ः is: (a) none — they are the same
   character (b) ह is a full letter that stands in the row and carries अ; ः is a
   dependent sign that only follows an akṣara (c) ः can begin a word (d) ह is only
   decorative
7. हिमालय is: (a) an unanalyzable ancient name (b) हिम + आलय, "snow-abode" — and
   English *Himalaya* is a loanword from Sanskrit (c) a cognate of English *home* (d)
   readable only with conjuncts
8. Reading check — write the English meaning of each: (a) गृह (b) इह (c) हसति

<details><summary>उत्तराणि · Answer Key</summary>

1. (b) /ɦ/ — voiced glottal fricative; the throat buzzes through it (§5). ((a) is §12's
   mistake 1 — that voiceless breath is the visarga's job.)
2. (b) the ūṣman — the traditional grouping; the phonetic distinction stands beside it,
   both true as what they are (§4).
3. (b) silence during ः (voiceless), buzz during ह (voiced) — the throat switch (§5, §9).
4. (b) 13 + 33 + 2 — the count promised in v1.c01.l02, completed today (§8). ((a) is
   the old classroom convenience.)
5. (b) intervocalic ह dropped — §12 mistake 2; the fix is the murmur bridge, slow.
6. (b) letter vs sign — ह stands alone, ः only rides (§12, §15).
7. (b) हिम + आलय "snow-abode"; English borrowed the name — a loan, not a cognate (§13).
8. (a) गृह = "house"; (b) इह = "here"; (c) हसति = "laughs" (§14).
</details>

sections.name: Revision
sections.markdown:
पुनरावृत्तिः — one screen to remember.

> **The letter:** ह /ɦ/ — voiced breath, open throat, mouth borrowed from the next
> vowel. **The switch:** ः voiceless, ह voiced — the hand on the throat referees. **The
> traps:** never devoice ह into English house-h; never drop it between vowels — म-ही,
> बा-हु. **The class:** traditionally ऊष्मन् with श ष स; phonetically not a sibilant —
> both true. **The completion:** 13 + 33 + 2, every square filled; the full recital is
> now yours. **The words:** fourteen, हिमालय and गृह leading. **The promise:** नमस्ते is
> three-quarters readable — the स्-joining opens Chapter 5.

Spaced review (distributed practice beats cramming [REF:cepeda2006]):

- **In 1 day:** re-take the dictation (exercise 3) cold; write the varṇamālā from
  memory once, checking against §8; read the story aloud, every ह voiced.
- **In 1 week:** lesson 4 is the Alphabet Exam — the varṇamālā written from memory in 8
  minutes is its centerpiece, and the sentence set returns in the reading task.
- **From now on:** the recital is a pocket-sized daily practice — once a day, accuracy
  first, anywhere. It is the whole sound system in forty seconds.

sections.name: Homework
sections.markdown:
गृहकार्यम् — about 30 minutes total. (Notice: for the first time you can read this
heading's root — गृह is today's word.)

1. **(10 min)** Finish exercises 3 and 4 if not completed in class: the dictation pass
   and the tracing sheet through the sentence row.
2. **(5 min)** The throat switch and murmur bridge (§9 drills 1–2) at a mirror; finish
   with मही, बाहु, इह — no ह dropped.
3. **(10 min, real world)** The ह hunt: on Hindi signs and headlines, find four words
   containing ह. Say each two ways — fast Hindi style, then careful Sanskrit style with
   the ह fully voiced and present. Bring your finds to class.
4. **(5 min, teach-back)** Teach someone the throat switch: hand on throat, अः vs हा,
   silence vs buzz. Then recite the complete varṇamālā to them, slowly — the first time
   you perform the whole alphabet for another human being. Take the applause; you earned
   all 48 pieces of it.

Tomorrow, before anything else: the 1-day re-dictation (§20). The gap is the method.

sections.name: Teacher Notes
sections.markdown:
शिक्षक-टिप्पणी

**Two summits, in order — and stage the second deliberately.** First the sound: fast,
because breathy voice is Chapter 3 machinery and ह is that machinery simplified. Then
the completion. Keep the wall chart out of sight during the sound work. Stage it like
pa-varga staged its sentences: silence first; chart up, one cell empty; a student writes
ह into it; say the numbers aloud — thirteen, thirty-three, two — and start the recital
without further commentary. The room will understand before you name it. Then name it:
every square, theirs.

**Timing plan (45 min):** §3 retrieval, written (5) → hook + throat switch demo on
अः/हा (5) → ह sound lab: murmur bridge, intervocalic words, ह/ः pair test (8) → writing
ह: board demo, air-writing, tracing start (6) → word list in pairs, throat-hands on (6)
→ THE COMPLETION: wall chart, last cell, first full recital — teacher leads group by
group, class echoes (10) → exercise 5 quick-fire (3) → homework briefing incl. the
1-day re-dictation (2).

**The ह/ः confusion is the week's real enemy.** Both get called "the breath", so insist
on the two absolutes: voiced vs voiceless (hand on throat), letter vs sign (stands alone
vs only rides). The pair test converts doubters faster than explanation.

**Differentiation:** Hindi-literate learners know the glyph and the sound — load them
with the intervocalic discipline (मही, बाहु, the कहना-habit) and make them dictation
referees. English-habit learners need the voicing: *ahead*, not *house*, and the throat
hand until it is boring. Heritage chanters may already own the recital — give them the
accuracy checklist and the recorder role, and hold everyone to pause form.

**What students find hard:** keeping the voice on through a breath (whispered ह is just
ः — the throat-hand catches it); slowing the recital down on completion day; believing a
letter with "nothing to do" still needs drilling. The intervocalic words convince them:
say मही fast and the ह simply vanishes — the drill is what keeps it.

Lesson video, ~6 min, presenter + motion graphics.

1. **Hook (0:00–0:30):** the varṇamālā wall chart, every cell lit except one, pulsing
   empty. A breath sound. ह fades in. Caption: "One letter left." Title card: हकारः —
   H and the Complete Alphabet.
2. **The sound (0:30–1:45):** presenter, hand on throat: अः (silence icon) vs हा (buzz
   icon animates). The ʱ-family callback: घ भ release-murmurs morph into standalone ह.
3. **The words (1:45–2:50):** हिमालय assembles from हिम + आलय over a stylized snow
   peak; caption "a loan the whole world took". गृह walks a timeline arrow into घर.
4. **Writing (2:50–3:25):** stroke panels animate ह; quick inset: ह vs ः, "letter vs
   sign" stamped.
5. **THE COMPLETION (3:25–5:10):** the screen quiets. The chart fills band by band as
   the recital audio plays; the last cell clicks in. The counts stamp on: 13 + 33 + 2.
   Beat of silence. Caption: "Every square. Yours."
6. **Recap + CTA (5:10–6:00):** the नमस्ते tracker: न ✓ म ✓ स ✓ ते ✓ — the joining
   glows dim, labeled "Chapter 5". End card: "Next: पुनरावृत्तिः — the Alphabet Exam.
   Bring a blank page and 8 minutes."

sections.name: Voice-over Script
sections.markdown:
Narration for the lesson video (§24). Sanskrit terms carry IPA cues in [brackets]; the
narrator reads them as IPA, not as English spelling.

- **00:00** Look at this chart. Every sound of Sanskrit — and one empty square. Listen:
  ha [ɦɐ]. The sound of breath itself, with the voice still humming inside it.
- **00:30** Hand on your throat. A voiceless puff — aḥ [ɐh] — nothing under your hand.
  Now switch the voice on: hā [ɦɑː]. Feel the buzz? That is the whole lesson. The
  visarga you have known for two chapters is this sound's voiceless twin.
- **01:10** You have made this sound before — inside gha [gʱɐ] and bha [bʱɐ], that
  murmured release. Delete the stop. What remains — ha [ɦɐ] — is today's letter.
- **01:45** Now read a word the world knows: himālaya [ɦimɑːlɐjɐ]. Snow — hima — and
  abode — ālaya. The snow-abode. English borrowed the name whole; today you read it in
  its own script. And this small word: gṛha [gr̩ɦɐ] — house. Say it slowly, then say
  your own word for home: ghar. Same word — twenty centuries apart.
- **02:50** Writing time. One flowing body — hook, bowl, the curl with its little tick —
  then the headline. No stem on the right. And never confuse the letter with the two
  dots: ha stands alone; the visarga only rides.
- **03:25** And now — quiet. Thirteen vowels. Two signs that ride. Twenty-five stops.
  ya ra la va [jɐ ɾɐ lɐ ʋɐ]. śa ṣa sa [ɕɐ ʂɐ sɐ] — and ha [ɦɐ]. (The recital plays;
  the chart fills.)
- **05:00** Thirteen. Thirty-three. Two. That count was a promise made in the second
  lesson of this course. Today it is kept — every square on this map is yours.
- **05:20** One promise remains: namaste [n̪ɐmɐst̪eː] — three of its four pieces are
  yours; the joining of s to te opens Chapter 5. Next: the whole alphabet, from memory,
  against the clock. Bring a blank page.

sections.name: Reel Script
sections.markdown:
40–50 seconds, vertical, captions burned in.

- **Hook (0:00–0:07):** extreme close-up, hand on throat. "The last letter of the
  Sanskrit alphabet is the sound of your own breath."
- **Demo (0:07–0:28):** "Voiceless —" aḥ [ɐh], silence icon. "Voiced —" hā [ɦɑː], buzz
  icon shakes. "Feel the switch? Sanskrit writes both: the sign ः and the letter ह."
  Quick beat: himālaya [ɦimɑːlɐjɐ] over a snow peak — "you can now read the name of the
  highest place on Earth."
- **Payoff (0:28–0:43):** the wall chart fills band by band at speed; the last cell
  clicks in: ह. Stamp: "13 + 33 + 2 — complete." Caption: "Learners of this course just
  finished the entire alphabet."
- **CTA (0:43–0:50):** "This is Sanskritam. Next: the whole alphabet from memory in 8
  minutes — the Alphabet Exam. Follow and take it with us." (End card: हकारः — the last
  letter.)

quiz.questions_markdown:
प्रश्नाः — answers in the key at the end; no peeking mid-quiz.

1. The sound of ह is: (a) a voiceless breath, like English *house*-h, in all positions
   (b) /ɦ/ — a breath with the voice buzzing through it (c) a sibilant like स (d) a
   vowel
2. According to the traditional classification, ह belongs to: (a) the antaḥstha, with
   य र ल व (b) the ūṣman class श ष स ह — though phonetically it is not a sibilant
   (c) the प-वर्ग (d) the vowels
3. Hand on your throat through रामः and then हरि. You should feel: (a) a buzz during
   both breaths (b) silence during the ः breath, a buzz during ह (c) a buzz during ः
   only (d) nothing in either
4. The completed varṇamālā counts: (a) 14 vowels + 32 consonants (b) 13 vowels + 33
   consonants + 2 ayogavāha (c) 13 vowels + 33 consonants, nothing else (d) 50 letters,
   all one category
5. A learner reads मही as [mɐiː] and बाहु as [bɑːu]. What happened? (a) nothing — both
   are correct (b) the ह between vowels was dropped — a Hindi fast-speech habit (c) the
   vowel lengths were wrong (d) the words contain conjuncts
6. In writing, the difference between ह and ः is: (a) none — they are the same
   character (b) ह is a full letter that stands in the row and carries अ; ः is a
   dependent sign that only follows an akṣara (c) ः can begin a word (d) ह is only
   decorative
7. हिमालय is: (a) an unanalyzable ancient name (b) हिम + आलय, "snow-abode" — and
   English *Himalaya* is a loanword from Sanskrit (c) a cognate of English *home* (d)
   readable only with conjuncts
8. Reading check — write the English meaning of each: (a) गृह (b) इह (c) हसति
quiz.answer_key_markdown:
1. (b) /ɦ/ — voiced glottal fricative; the throat buzzes through it (§5). ((a) is §12's
   mistake 1 — that voiceless breath is the visarga's job.)
2. (b) the ūṣman — the traditional grouping; the phonetic distinction stands beside it,
   both true as what they are (§4).
3. (b) silence during ः (voiceless), buzz during ह (voiced) — the throat switch (§5, §9).
4. (b) 13 + 33 + 2 — the count promised in v1.c01.l02, completed today (§8). ((a) is
   the old classroom convenience.)
5. (b) intervocalic ह dropped — §12 mistake 2; the fix is the murmur bridge, slow.
6. (b) letter vs sign — ह stands alone, ः only rides (§12, §15).
7. (b) हिम + आलय "snow-abode"; English borrowed the name — a loan, not a cognate (§13).
8. (a) गृह = "house"; (b) इह = "here"; (c) हसति = "laughs" (§14).

registers.text: The traditional ūṣman class is श ष स ह. Phonetically, श ष स are sibilants — noisy friction shaped by the tongue. ह is not a sibilant: its friction happens at the glottis, in the open throat, with the tongue doing nothing. The class grouping is the tradition's; the phonetic distinction is real; neither cancels the other. [REF:whitney1889 §§59–65]

The grammatical tradition's own name for the class explains the grouping: ऊष्मन् (ūṣman) means "heat, hot breath, steam" — these four are the breath-sounds, the ones you could warm your hands on. By breath, ह belongs completely.

ह is /ɦ/ — a voiced glottal fricative: strong airflow through the open glottis while the vocal folds keep vibrating in a slack, murmured mode. It is the breathy voice you built five times in Chapter 3 — the ʱ of घ झ ढ ध भ — standing alone, with no stop in front of it. [REF:ladefoged2015], [REF:whitney1889 §65]

विसर्ग ः /h/ and ह /ɦ/ are one gesture with the voice switched off and on: both push breath through an open throat. ः is voiceless — the hand on the throat feels nothing; ह is voiced — the hand feels a buzz the whole way through. [REF:whitney1889 §65]

The inventory is complete: 13 vowels + 33 consonants + 2 ayogavāha — exactly the counts promised in v1.c01.l02, now owned letter by letter. The two ayogavāha keep their honest label: categorically neither vowels nor consonants, they only ever lean on a vowel (v1.c02.l06). [REF:whitney1889 §§19–75]

हिमालय is a transparent compound: हिम (hima) "snow" + आलय (ālaya) "abode, dwelling" — "the abode of snow". And English *Himalaya* is a genuine **loanword**: English borrowed the mountain range's Sanskrit name whole — like *yoga* and *karma*, a loan, not a cognate. [REF:apte1890 s.v. हिमालय]
Sanskrit गृह is the ancestor of Hindi घर: the modern word descends from the ancient one through the regular sound changes of Indo-Aryan. [REF:masica1991]

With ह, the letter inventory is closed: 46 letters and 2 signs. Everything else you will ever read on a Sanskrit page is built from these by combination — the mātrā forms you already command, and the consonant joinings (conjuncts) that Chapter 5 opens. New combinations are coming; new letters are not. [REF:whitney1889 §§19–75]
As dictionary words: हरि means "tawny, bay-colored" among other senses, and is a proper name; हर means "taking away, removing, seizing", and is a proper name. [REF:apte1890 s.v. हरि]
In the devotional tradition हरि is a beloved name of Viṣṇu and हर of Śiva — paired to this day in the compound हरिहर (harihara). In this lesson both are vocabulary, doing honest secular work.
